title: Would God Ever Say, ‘I Will Save You No More’?
summary: Our hope doesn’t rest on the sincerity of our repentance, as important as that is. Our hope ultimately rests on the compassion of our God.
summary_zh: 父母知道,并不是每一个“对不起”都是相同的。 有时“对不起”的意思是“对不起我被抓了”或“对不起我正面临后果 ” 。 然而,有时这意味着“我错了。 你会原谅我吗?
title_zh: 神是否会说：“我不再拯救你了”？
content: Parents know that not every “I’m sorry” is the same. Sometimes “I’m sorry” means “I’m sorry I got caught” or “I’m sorry I’m facing the consequences.” Yet sometimes it means “I was wrong. Will you forgive me?” Parents also don’t respond to every apology the same way. Sometimes we immediately embrace our child. Other times we slow the conversation down. We ask questions. We press a little deeper, because we don’t just want to hear the words “I’m sorry.” We want those words to reflect a changed heart. In Judges 10, we encounter shocking words. The Lord says, “I will save you no more. Go and cry out to the gods whom you have chosen; let them save you in the time of your distress” (vv. 13–14). Would God ever speak words like that to us ? Like a good parent, God knows there are different kinds of “I’m sorry,” and he’s not satisfied with words alone. He sometimes speaks to his people in surprising ways because he’s after our hearts. Lord’s Holy Rebuke The book of Judges follows a familiar pattern. Israel sins. The Lord gives them over to their enemies. They cry out. Then the Lord raises up a deliverer (e.g., 2:10–16). But that pattern isn’t merely a repeating cycle—it’s a downward spiral. Like a good parent, God knows there are different kinds of ‘I’m sorry,’ and he’s not satisfied with words alone. By Judges 10, Israel has descended deeper into idolatry than ever before. No longer content to run after the gods of the Canaanites, they’ve collected gods from every surrounding nation. Consequently, their existence hangs in the balance as their enemies move into Israel’s heartland. Yet as Israel’s sin and misery reaches a new low, their confession reaches a new height. For the first time in Judges, Israel confesses their sin (v. 10). But apparently, the Lord has heard this speech before . He knows when “I’m sorry” is little more than words. So instead of raising up another deliverer, he reminds Israel of his repeated acts of salvation (vv. 11–12). Then comes the striking statement: “I will save you no more” (v. 13). Those words should unsettle us. They certainly would’ve unsettled Israel. God’s words expose their dangerous presumption. For generations, Israel assumed the pattern would continue. They thought they could repeatedly forsake the Lord and simply return to him whenever life became unbearable. But not this time. The Lord’s rebuke shatters their assumption. You chose your gods. Cry out to them. Let them save you. The Lord exposes both their idols’ emptiness and their hearts’ audacity. Their gods cannot save them. And the Lord won’t be treated as an emergency deliverer while his people give themselves to other gods. Moreover, the Lord’s rebuke isn’t just for Israel. It’s meant to confront us today. These words were written for our instruction (1 Cor. 10:11). We also shouldn’t assume we can cling to our idols, live in our sin, ignore God’s commands, and then simply cry out to him when life falls apart. God isn’t manipulated by empty words. His rebuke exposes our idols and confronts our presumption. He calls us to repentance. Lord’s Compassion When the Lord rebukes Israel, they finally move beyond mere words to genuine repentance. They put away the foreign gods and serve the Lord (v. 16). As soon as they do, we read, “[The Lord] became impatient over the misery of Israel.” Or we might translate it, “He could bear Israel’s suffering no longer” (v. 16, JB). One of the most shocking verses in Judges is followed by one of its most beautiful. The God who rightly opposes sin is also moved by his people’s suffering. The God who says “I will save you no more” is the same God who only bears his people’s misery for so long. Certainly, this passage calls for genuine repentance. Yet when it explains God’s response, it doesn’t point us first to Israel’s motivation but to God’s . It doesn’t say, “Israel’s heart was finally sincere.” It says, “[The LORD] became impatient over the misery of Israel.” Our hope doesn’t rest on the sincerity of our repentance, as important as that is. Our hope ultimately rests on the compassion of our God. We need both parts of this passage. If we’ve grown comfortable with sin and presume on God’s grace, we need God’s holy rebuke. But if we’re crushed beneath the weight of our failures, if we know our repentance falls short and wonder if God is finished with us, then we need a reminder that the God who refuses to overlook sin also refuses to bear his people’s misery forever. God’s compassion moves him to save. Holiness and Compassion of the Cross This tension we feel between God’s holiness and his compassionate love finds its fulfillment at the cross. There, God’s holiness wasn’t set aside—and neither was his compassion. At the cross, God’s holy rebuke fell. His wrath was poured out—but not on us. Instead, it fell on his Son. God’s compassion was displayed as the sinless One bore the full rebuke our sin deserves that we might receive the love we never deserved. Our hope doesn’t rest on the sincerity of our repentance, as important as that is. Our hope ultimately rests on the compassion of our God. Then, after rising from the dead, Christ pours out his Spirit on us, renews our hearts, and enables us to do what Israel never fully did—put away our idols and serve the Lord. Parents know that “I’m sorry” isn’t always the same. Our Heavenly Father knows too. He refuses to settle for empty words. Yet when his people truly return to him, they don’t find a reluctant Father. They find a God rich in mercy. Let’s return to the Lord whose holy rebuke leads us to repentance and whose compassionate love moves him to save.
content_zh:
父母知道,并不是每一个“对不起”都是相同的。 有时“对不起”的意思是“对不起我被抓了”或“对不起我正面临后果 ” 。 然而,有时这意味着“我错了。 你会原谅我吗?” 父母对道歉的反应也不相同。 有时我们马上拥抱我们的孩子。 其他时候,我们慢下来的对话。 我们问问题。
因为我们并不想听到“对不起”的话。 我们希望这些话能反映改变的心意。 在法官10中,我们遇到令人震惊的言论。 主说:我不会再拯救你们了。 去呼喊你们所选择的神灵吧,在你们受难的时候,让他们拯救你们吧。” 上帝会这样对我们说话吗?
像一个好父母一样,上帝知道有各种不同的“对不起”,他并不满足于单词。 他有时会以令人惊讶的方式与人民交谈, 主的圣训 法官书遵循一种熟悉的模式。 以色列的罪过 主把他们交给敌人 他们喊出来。 然后耶和华举起一个送货人(例如2:10-16).
但这种模式不仅仅是一个重复循环,而是螺旋式的下降。 与好父母一样,上帝知道有不同种类的‘对不起', 10号法官指出,以色列比以往更深地陷入偶像崇拜。 他们不再满足于追逐迦南人的神,
因此,当他们的敌人进入以色列的心脏地带时,他们的生存是平衡的。 然而,随着以色列的罪恶和苦难达到一个新的低点,他们的忏悔达到了一个新的高度。 在法官中,以色列首次承认他们的罪过(v.10)。 但很明显,上帝以前听过这个演讲 他知道, " 我很抱歉 " 只不过是言语而已。
因此,他没有培养另一个送货人,而是提醒以色列他一再的救赎行为(vv.11-12). 接下来是令人惊讶的声明:“我将不再拯救你们”(v.13)。 这些话应该使我们不安。 他们肯定会让以色列不安。 上帝的话暴露了他们的危险的假设。 几代人以来,以色列一直认为这种模式会继续下去。
他们以为他们可以反复抛弃主,只要生命变得无法忍受,就干脆回到他身边. 但这次不行 主的谴责打破了他们的假设。 你选择了自己的神 哭他们。 让他们救你。 主揭露他们的偶像是空虚的, 他们的神不能拯救他们。
上帝不会被当作紧急运送者, 而且,上帝的谴责不仅仅是针对以色列的。 今天, 这些文字是为我们的指示而写(1 Cor. 10:11). 也不应该认为我们可以坚持我们的偶像,
上帝不是空话所操纵的。 他的斥责暴露了我们的偶像,并对抗了我们的推测. 他要求我们忏悔 主的同情心 当上帝斥责以色列时,他们终于超越了单纯的言辞而真正悔改。 他们收走外国神祇,为主服务(v.16).
他们一听我们就说:'主啊!'对于以色列的苦难,我们便变得不耐烦。 或者我们可以翻译为:"他可以忍受以色列不再遭受苦难"(v.16, JB). 法官中最令人震惊的诗句之一紧随其后,是其最美丽的诗句之一。 正确反对罪恶的上帝也因人民的痛苦而感动。
说"我不会再救你了"的上帝,就是只承受人民如此长久苦难的上帝. 当然,这段话需要真正的忏悔。 但当它解释上帝的反应时, 它并不首先指向以色列的动机,
“以色列心里终于真心实意。 它说:“耶和华对于以色列的苦难变得不耐烦。” 我们的希望并不在于我们悔改的诚意, 我们的希望最终取决于我们上帝的同情。 我们需要这段话的两部分。 如果我们对罪恶感到自在,
但是如果我们被压在失败的阴影下, 如果我们知道我们的忏悔不足, 上帝的怜悯感动他去拯救。
宗座和对十字的同情 我们感到上帝的圣洁和慈悲的爱之间的这种紧张, 在那里,上帝的圣洁没有被抛在一边,他的慈悲也没有。 在十字架上,上帝的神圣责难降临. 他的愤怒被激怒了,但不是对我们。 相反,它落在他儿子身上。
上帝的慈悲被展现为无罪之徒 我们罪孽深重 罪有应得 得到我们从未得到的爱 我们的希望并不在于我们悔改的诚意, 我们的希望最终取决于我们上帝的同情。
然后,基督从死里复活后,把他的精神倾注在我们的身上,使我们的心灵复活,使我们能做以色列从未做过的事,即抛弃我们的偶像,崇拜主。 父母知道“对不起”并不总是一样。 我们的天父也知道 他拒绝为空话和解. 当他的族人真正回到他身边时,
他们发现一个仁慈的上帝 让我们回到上帝身边,

title: When You Need a Christmas Miracle
summary: We won’t find all our struggles tied up with a neat bow like the gifts under our trees. But God, our Immanuel, will be with us through it all.
summary_zh: 故你应当宣读,主将给你一个迹象。 看 哪 、 处 女 必 孕 育 子 、 起 名 叫 以 曼 奴 (以萨. 7:14 反射 如果你今年看几部节日电影, 庆典季节显然具有神奇的能力,可以把灵魂伴侣聚集在一起,拯救家庭企业,治愈无法治愈的疾病。 12月25日一转,不可能实现。
title_zh: 当您需要圣诞奇迹时
content: Read Therefore the Lord himself will give you a sign. Behold, the virgin shall conceive and bear a son, and shall call his name Immanuel. (Isa. 7:14) Reflect If you watch even a few holiday movies this year, you’ll encounter the trope of the “Christmas miracle.” The festive season apparently has the magical ability to bring soulmates together, rescue floundering family businesses, and heal incurable diseases. The impossible becomes possible when December 25 rolls around. The nation of Judah in Isaiah’s day was in dire need of a miracle. They were in a centuries-long cycle of sin and rebellion against God. The northern kingdom of Israel had joined forces with Syria, and together they threatened to attack. Judah’s evil king, Ahaz, wouldn’t submit to God. What hope did they have? The impossible becomes possible when December 25 rolls around. Despite Ahaz’s hard-heartedness, God shows grace by making a promise: “The Lord himself will give you a sign. Behold, the virgin shall conceive and bear a son, and shall call his name Immanuel” (Isa. 7:14). Later, in Matthew’s Gospel, we learn that “Immanuel” means “God with us” (Matt. 1:23). A spark of light appears in Judah’s dark future. But it didn’t seem like it could happen. A virgin bearing a son? Impossible. God dwelling among sinful people? Impossible. Yet this is what we celebrate at Christmas. Matthew recounts Jesus’s birth and tells us that “all this took place to fulfill what the Lord had spoken by the prophet” (v. 22)—Christ is the ultimate fulfillment of God’s promise through Isaiah. God did the impossible. What seems impossible to you this Christmas? You may have a list of tasks, commitments, and events so long that you can’t possibly get it all done—let alone with a sense of peace, contentment, or even sanity. You may be facing family conflict, and you don’t know how to begin healing the divides. You may be grieving, and the prospect of finding any holiday joy seems remote. God doesn’t promise to do everything that seems impossible. On Christmas morning, we won’t find all our struggles tied up with a neat bow like the gifts under our trees. But God, our Immanuel, will be with us through it all. Impossible as it once seemed, God himself “came into the world to save sinners” (1 Tim. 1:15). He’s with us now by his Spirit, and one day he’ll return to make a new world and dwell with us physically and eternally. We won’t find all our struggles tied up with a neat bow like the gifts under our trees. But God, our Immanuel, will be with us through it all. So this Advent season, look to your God who does the impossible. Pray earnestly for peace and rest, for healing, for reconciliation, for joy. But remember he has already given us what we need. He’s redefined what’s impossible: “Neither death nor life, nor angels nor rulers, nor things present nor things to come, nor powers, nor height nor depth, nor anything else in all creation, will be able to separate us from the love of God in Christ Jesus our Lord” (Rom. 8:38–39). It’s impossible that he’ll abandon us. Because God is steadfastly with us, we can face what seems insurmountable this Christmas. Our weaknesses and sins will not hinder God’s determination to save and dwell among his people. He is God with us, now and forever, as the apostle John sees in his vision of the future: “Behold, the dwelling place of God is with man. He will dwell with them, and they will be his people, and God himself will be with them as their God” (Rev. 21:3). Respond What impossible situation are you facing this Christmas? Spend time praying about that today. Consider what we learn about the Lord from these verses and how that changes the way you think about your struggles or fears. What difference does it make that God is with you?

title: What Roman History Can (and Can’t) Explain About Christianity
summary: ‘Rome’s Age of Revolution’ is a tightly argued book that makes a number of important connections between the Greco-Roman world and the formation of the early church.
summary_zh: 罗马革命时代的矛盾和紧张局势中,没有任何一个比这本书及其尘埃覆盖层的对比更引人注目。 这并非作者Tim Whitmarsh的过错, 出版商也从未夸大某一论文的新奇性、原创性、争议甚至丑闻, 但它仍然是罐子。 而这产生了无法实现的期望的不幸效果,它把一本清晰,简短,写得很好,深思熟虑,而且完全合理的书变成了轻微的失望.
title_zh: 罗马历史能够（和不能够）为基督教做出哪些解释
content: Of all the paradoxes and tensions in Rome’s Age of Revolution , none is so striking as the contrast between the book and its dustcover. That’s not the fault of the author, Tim Whitmarsh, currently regius professor of Greek at the University of Cambridge. Nor is it unheard of for publishers to exaggerate the novelty, originality, controversy, or even scandal of a particular thesis, especially when promoting scholarly arguments to a wider audience. But it jars nonetheless. And it has the unfortunate effect of creating undeliverable expectations, which turn a clear, brief, well-written, thoughtful, and perfectly reasonable book into a slight disappointment. “This remarkable book redefines early Christianity,” proclaims the first endorsement on the back cover. “Dazzling. This thrilling and elegantly written book will change how you see Rome, and Christianity, for ever,” says the next. The breathlessness continues. Harry Sidebottom says it “makes us rethink everything we know about the rise of Christianity.” Candida Moss commends it for “for ever changing how we think about the entanglement of empire, culture and early Christianity.” The inside jacket has fewer references to “everything” and “for ever,” but praise for the book’s originality continues: “Offers a whole new way to view Christians as an integrated part of the whole, multifaceted ancient Mediterranean world.” And so forth. There’s nothing wrong with rave reviews and ringing endorsements, of course. The problem in this case is that they lead the reader to anticipate a fresh, bold, provocative, and potentially explosive new argument, which is exactly what Rome’s Age of Revolution: Augustus, Empire, and the Making of Christianity doesn’t provide. What it offers instead is a measured, straightforward, run-of-the-mill presentation of a widely accepted view—that Christianity “was decisively and fundamentally shaped by the culture that incubated it” (228), both Greek and Roman, and “could not have come into being in anything like the form we know it without the revolutionary impact of Augustus’ political reforms” (230)—to a nonspecialist audience. Little in here is new, or claims to be. Plenty of it is found embryonically in Eusebius, Chrysostom, Thomas Aquinas, and John Calvin, to say nothing of F. F. Bruce or N. T. Wright. Integration and Conflict Whitmarsh revels in nuance, not controversy. “From one perspective, Christianity changed everything. From another, it reflected the world around it” (xxiv). It would be simplistic, for example, to frame an argument in terms of Greco-Roman cultural influence on early Christianity, because influence flows both ways. It would be equally simplistic to point out all the ways in which the ante-Nicene church aped and adapted imperial Rome without noting the ways in which they had nothing to do with each other: “There was very little that was Augustan about, for example, the Eucharist” (231). Similarly, although “most Christians were fully integrated into Roman society, and no more or less harassed than anyone else” (184), and although many stories of Christian martyrdom were stylized, embellished, or even invented, there’s no doubt that emperors like Decius and Diocletian pursued “systematic, pan-imperial action” and “vindictively anti-Christian policies” (186) and that “Christian zealots were certainly executed” (204). His analogy is apt: Although we know that the representation of cowboys and Indians in a western movie is usually a cinematic distortion, it would be a mistake to assume on that basis that conflict between settlers and indigenous peoples in North America in the nineteenth century was entirely the invention of Hollywood. (203–4) The book is at its best in parts 1 and 2, when describing the endlessly fascinating world of the late Roman republic and early Roman empire, and the ways in which it made Christianity’s message comprehensible and its expansion possible. Roman Influence on Christianity The universal access to the gospel, for instance, would’ve been hard to imagine without the award of citizenship to all free males on the Italian peninsula, which is the moment “when Roman identity ceased to be tied geographically to the city of Rome itself, and began to be associated more with loyalty to an idea” (4). The book is at its best when describing the ways in which the Roman world made Christianity’s message comprehensible and its expansion possible. The story of Luke-Acts is that of a Roman road trip, set in a world in which Homeric seaways have been replaced by Augustan highways. The paradigmatic Christian form of literature was the letter, which likewise depended on safe roads, milestones, and transport infrastructure. We could go on: Roman laws, aqueducts, bridges, provinces, and architecture all reconfigured the concept of space in ways that shaped the early Christian movement. In related ways, “Augustus’ revolution reset time as well as space” (77). The arrival of Augustus signified a new world order, complete with a new calendar centered on his person and a sense that the old age had passed and a new one arrived. Not only that, but “the earliest Christians seem to have used a characteristically Augustan approach to time” (112), regarding themselves as the fulfillment of Jewish prophecies much as (say) Virgil saw the Romans as the true heirs of Homeric Greece. Readers may quibble with Whitmarsh’s use of “supersessionism” in this context, but the comparison is fascinating and well drawn. When we situate the early church within this world, its growth, influence, and missionary strategy all make good historical sense, as Whitmarsh shows in part 3. Within Greco-Roman communities, and cities in particular, Christian leaders would have been recognizable as Charismatics, religious experimenters competing for success within a deregulated religious market; as Experts, presenting themselves as philosophers with “a coherent system of wisdom that competed with, indeed far outdid, the various Greek philosophical schools” (148); as Bibliophiles, writing and reading books because they operated in a literate world; and as Zealots, with their violent and heroic stories of martyrdom. There are even points of overlap between Greek novels and early Christian thought, once again with influence flowing in both directions. Occasional Overstatements Though the book is generally balanced in tone, occasionally it strays into overstatement or factual error. It’s a stretch to say that Jesus’s original teachings are “lost forever” because we only have them in Greek translation (xix); it’s simply untrue to say that “we do not, of course, have a single word securely attributed to Jesus, who spoke only Aramaic” (37), in light of well-known examples like “talitha koum,” “ephphatha,” “Abba,” “Cephas,” “Boanerges,” “mammon,” and “Eloi, Eloi, lema sabachthani.” To be fair, some of Whitmarsh’s overstatements are standard fare among classicists who aren’t Christians: “The fact that the Christmas story is a fiction is well understood, and has been for hundreds of years” (92). Though the book is generally balanced in tone, occasionally it strays into overstatement or factual error. But some overstatements are more surprising and would be rejected by many in the scholarly guild: “It is a theme central to the theology of the Gospels: that the coming of Jesus . . . renders Jewish law obsolete” (111). Equally puzzling is his belief that Christians only met in private homes, not least because it comes right after citing a work (by my doctoral supervisor, no less) that demonstrates the reverse to be true. Some errors are inexplicable, especially for a professor of Greek. His claim that “slave” is the dominant meaning of diakonos in the Septuagint (144) is completely upside down; diakonos only appears a handful of times, and never to translate eved , for which the translators usually use doulos or pais . More baffling still is the idea that the author of 1 Corinthians 7:3–5 was characte

这本令人兴奋和优雅的书将改变你对罗马和永远的基督教的看法。” 气息持续.
Harry Sidebottin说这“让我们重新思考我们对基督教兴起的一切了解。 ” 坎迪达 摩斯称赞它“永远改变我们对帝国、文化和早期基督教的纠缠。 ” 内部夹克很少提到"一切"和"永远",但对该书原创性的赞美仍然在继续:"提出全新的方法,将基督徒视为一丝不苟.
整个多元的古地中海世界的一部分。” 及诸众生. 当然,
问题在于它们让读者预见到一个新的、大胆的、挑衅性的和潜在的爆炸性的新论点,这正是罗马革命时代的道理:奥古斯都、帝国和基督教的造就。
相反,它所提供的是一种有分寸、直截了当、一成不变的观点,即基督教 " 由孕育它的文化决定性和根本地塑造 " (228年),希腊语和罗马语,以及 " 在没有奥古斯都政治改革的革命影响的情况下,不可能以我们所知的形式出现 " (230年) -- -- 一个非专家学者。
. 里面的小东西是新来的,或者自称是 在尤塞比乌斯、克莱索斯托姆、托马斯·阿奎纳斯和约翰·加尔文等地发现很多胚胎,更不用说F. F. Bruce或N. T. Wright。 融合与冲突 Whitmarsh 在细微的,没有争议。 “从一个角度看,基督教改变了一切。 从另一个角度看,它反映了它周围的世界”(二十四)。
例如,从格雷科-罗马文化对早期基督教的影响的角度来描述一个论点,是过于简单化的,因为影响是双向流动的。
同样简单的是,指出前好教堂如何发展并改造了帝国罗马,而没有指出它们与彼此无关的方式:“奥古斯坦对例如欧查尔主义者来说是很少的”(231)。
同样,虽然“大多数基督徒完全融入了罗马社会,而且没有比任何其他人受到多少骚扰”(184年),虽然许多关于基督教殉教的故事被刻画、装饰甚至发明,但毫无疑问,德修斯和迪奥克莱蒂安等皇帝推行“系统化、泛帝国主义行动”和“可信的反基督教政策”(186年),以及“基督教教条”
许多人被处决”(204)。 他的类比是恰当的:虽然我们知道牛仔和印第安人在西部电影中的代表通常是一种电影的歪曲,但在此基础上假设十九世纪北美定居者和土著人之间的冲突完全是好莱坞的发明,那就是错误的了.
(203–4) 这本书在第一部分和第二部分中表现得最好,描述了罗马共和国后期和罗马帝国早期无休止的迷人世界,以及它如何使基督教的信息可以理解和扩展.
罗马对基督教的影响 例如,如果没有意大利半岛上所有自由男性的公民权,那么普遍获得福音是很难想象的。 此时,“罗马身份在地理上不再与罗马城本身联系在一起,开始更多地与对一个思想的忠诚联系在一起。”
在描述罗马世界如何使基督教的信息可以理解和扩展时,这本书是尽其所能的。 卢克-Acts的故事是一个罗马公路之旅的故事,设定于一个被奥古斯坦高速公路取代的霍斯克海道世界.
典型的基督教文学形式就是信,它同样依赖于安全的道路、里程碑和运输基础设施。 我们可以继续说:罗马法律、水管、桥梁、省道和建筑都以塑造早期基督教运动的方式重新塑造了空间的概念。 在相关方面, " 奥古斯都革命重新确定时间和空间 " (77)。
奥古斯都的到来标志着一个新的世界秩序,完成了以他个人为中心的新的日历,并感觉到老年已经过去,新的日历已经到来。
不仅如此,而且“最早的基督教徒似乎在时间问题上采用了奥古斯坦式的典型做法”(112年),自称是犹太预言的实现,因为(比如)维吉尔将罗马人视为霍斯里克希腊的真正继承人。 读者可能与Whitmarsh在此背景下使用“超会论”相提并论,
当我们坐落于这个世界上的早期教堂时,它的成长,影响和传教策略都具有良好的历史意义,正如惠特玛什在第3部分所示. 在Greco-Roman社区,特别是城市中,基督教领袖被承认为Charismatics, 宗教实验者在不受管制的宗教市场中竞争成功;
作为专家,把自己描绘成哲学家,“一个一致的智慧体系,它与希腊各哲学院校竞争,实际上远远超过了这些哲学院校”(148年);作为圣经,写作和阅读书籍,因为他们在一个识字的世界里运作;作为Zealots,他们充满暴力和英勇的殉难故事。
希腊小说和早期基督教思想之间甚至有重叠点,再次影响双向流动. 偶尔多报 虽然这本书在语气上一般是平衡的,但偶尔会误入多报或事实错误。 说耶稣的原始教义“永远消失”,
“当然,我们没有一个字可以安全地归结到耶稣身上,而耶稣只讲阿拉姆语”(37),这是完全不真实的,因为众所周知的例子有“塔利塔·库姆 ” 、 “埃夫法塔 ” 、 “阿布巴 ” 、 “塞法斯 ” 、 “波内热斯 ” 、 “马门 ” 、 “埃洛伊 、 埃洛伊 、 莱玛·萨巴赫塔尼 ” 。 简而言之,惠特玛什的一些夸大其词是那些不是基督徒的经典主义者的标准票价: "事实上,
圣诞故事是虚构的,是可以理解的,已有数百年历史”(92年)。 虽然这本书在语气上一般是平衡的,但偶尔会误入多报或事实错误。 但是,有些多报更令人吃惊,许多学者会拒绝:“这是福音神学的核心主题:耶稣的降临......。

title: Young Adults Are Hungry. Here Are 3 Ways to Feed Them.
summary: Gen Z’s hunger for food, people, and the Word gives the church a magnificent opportunity in this moment.
summary_zh: 当我们在Whaley街和Wayne街的拐角打开一个世纪以来的教堂大门时, 我们以为当晚我们会有大约50个人穿过它们。 毕竟是Gen Z的圣经课 有多少Zers将军真正想学习圣经? 显然,超过50个。 我们不得不找更多的椅子
title_zh: 青年人正处于饥饿状态。以下是满足他们需求的 3 种方法。
content: When we opened the century-old church doors on the corner of Whaley Street and Wayne Street, we figured we’d have about 50 folks step through them that night. It was a Bible class for Gen Z, after all. How many Gen Zers actually want to learn about the Bible? Apparently, more than 50. We had to scramble for more chairs. It quickly became obvious that this generation—my generation—is hungry for the Bible, and we’ll starve if we don’t get fed. How are you feeding the hungry young adults in your context? My church has learned key lessons about feeding college students and young adults. These aren’t novel, but I hope they can help your people as much as they’ve helped ours. 1. Food (Like, Actual Food) I was sitting across from a leader at a major university recently and asked him how we could influence the students on that campus. He looked at me and said the plainest thing: “Food wins.” To win the heart of a man, you go through the stomach. If you want to feed people the gospel, consider first feeding them a sandwich. This is why my brother (“Chef Chunk” as they call him) has been serving an incredible amount of pancake batter out of a four-foot plastic storage container, complete with chocolate chips, blueberries, and a few other cheap toppings. We start pancake-flipping before 7 p.m. and don’t stop until we start class at 8:03 p.m., to keep up with the demand. Apparently breakfast for dinner is a fan favorite. Eating meals with others is one of the greatest indicators of personal well-being—the more we eat with our families (whether spiritual or biological), the more likely we are to be satisfied with our lives and filled with love, joy, and peace. Yet we’re eating fewer meals together than ever. What if the church was one of the great combatants of this damaging trend? 2. Friends (Like, Actual Friends) Speaking of loneliness, our culture is increasingly lacking “third spaces” where lonely people can find and build community. Robert Putnam described and predicted this decades ago in Bowling Alone —but these days we don’t just bowl alone. We shop alone, eat alone, entertain alone. We even tend to date or do friendship “alone,” as in virtually rather than in person. What few third spaces remain—the gym, sports environments, coffee shops—aren’t ideal for making meaningful connections. In gyms, we have our headphones on; at sports games, the music is so loud you get hoarse when you speak; and coffee shops are great but usually filled with headphones-on, screened-off people (and $7 lattes). Fresh-out-of-college Jimmy has nowhere to meet potential-best-friend Johnny or potential-love-of-his-life Jessica. That leaves Jimmy feeling hopeless in one of the most foundational needs of life: relationships. Our culture is increasingly lacking ‘third spaces’ where lonely people can find and build community. Yet this is a hole best filled by the new humanity God created called the church. Amid a growing cultural hunger for embodied friendships, maybe one of the major ways our church can “seek the welfare” of our cities (Jer. 29:7) is to build environments where a wide variety of folks can congregate. Maybe that looks like creating spaces for line-dancing, pick-up basketball, or weekly pickleball nights. But I have a hunch that one of the most interesting third spaces we can create might not need to be about entertainment. 3. Knowledge (Like, Spiritual Knowledge) “Do you know what Christmas is about?” “Um—not sure. What do you mean?” “Like, do you know the story behind it?” “Hmm. I feel like it’s about a guy . . .” “YES! Do you know his name?” “Mmm. Nah man.” “Jesus. His name is Jesus.” This is a real conversation I had with an average high school student in the South, the heart of the so-called Bible Belt. I could tell you of dozens of other conversations just like it. Here’s the truth: The Bible is the most interesting story in the world, and no one knows it anymore. Christians have a tragic habit of making this story far less interesting than it should be, just as film adaptations have an uncanny ability to make some of the best stories ever written feel like spoonfuls of sawdust. But the truth remains: No story has ever been (or ever will be) better, truer, and more powerful than the Bible. No story has ever been (or ever will be) better, truer, and more powerful than the Bible. The marvelous thing about our age is that the Bible is interesting again—partly because it’s utterly novel. Do you want to know why Jordan Peterson could lecture on obscure stories from Genesis to sold-out crowds? Do you want to know why major streaming services are pumping out Bible films and TV series ? Do you want to know why Bible sales are through the roof in the last few years? Because our generation has never heard these stories before. Maybe one of the most captivating things the church can do is bring the Greatest Story Ever Told into the present moment. We certainly aren’t doing this perfectly in our church’s Gen-Z Bible class. Every time I teach, I feel as if I’ve failed miserably. J.T.—you blew it. You weren’t even close to explaining that right. I mean, how could you forget to include the Table of Nations before you reach Abram!? But though our sound systems have been off, our mics have gone in and out, our recording equipment hasn’t worked, our Spotify playlist has interrupted in the middle of sessions, our whiteboards have been too small, and our powerpoint slides have gotten jacked up—the Word of God is life. Students and young adults are flocking to understand how this magnificent writing we called the Book all fits together. These guys and gals don’t read much, but they long to read this book. They just feel intimidated. Wouldn’t you? Don’t you? The Bible is a complex book, and we’re past the days of assuming people understand it. Yet we’re also past the days of assuming we should simplify truth to satisfy the questions of curious new believers. If you listen closely, you can hear from young adults the same whisper of hunger, thirst, panting—perhaps even desperation—that we see on the lips of the Ethiopian eunuch when asked, “Do you understand what you are reading?” (Acts 8:30). “How can I, unless someone guides me?” (v. 31). In today’s age of Gemini, ChatGPT, and Claude, we may be tempted to assume anyone can teach themselves. But I wonder if the ubiquity of all-knowing machines actually makes the candor, emotion, and particularity of human knowledge and teaching that much more significant. The excess of knowledge brings more questions, not fewer. The excess of knowledge brings more questions, not fewer. Christian, be ready for a resurgence in questions—not just questions about dating, relationships, technology, and sexuality (all important) but questions about the Scriptures. This is a call for all of us to better ourselves in engaging with the Word of the Living God and to believe that this Word is even more valuable than fine gold (Ps. 19:10). It all reminds me of Amos’s famous prophecy: “‘Behold, the days are coming,’ declares the Lord GOD, ‘when I will send a famine on the land—not a famine of bread, nor a thirst for water, but of hearing the words of the LORD’” (8:11). This prophecy fits our times. Though we’re in a “famine” of biblical literacy as a generation and as a nation, the hunger for food, people, and the Word gives the church a magnificent opportunity in this moment.
